utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P284 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi. I think I still have to put on the record because it's not yet that the leave requested to reply to the response to the 92 ter motion, that that leave was granted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would also tender associated exhibits 65 ter 06908, 18244, and 22696.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Traldi, could we have a look at 65 ter 18244. Yes. I think that earlier there were redactions in it which are now not there anymore in the English version. Having verified this, Madam Registrar, 65 ter 06908 receives number ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P285, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P285 is admitted into evidence. 65 ter 18244 receives number ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P286, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P286 is admitted. 22696?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Becomes Exhibit P287, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Again looking at -- let me have a look. Yes, there is some handwriting on the original which is not identified as handwriting in the English translation, but perhaps the parties could look at it to see what it presents. It doesn't seem to be very important. Yes, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will now read a brief oral summary of the witness's evidence for the public record. Mevludin Sejmenovic was one of the founders of the Party of Democratic Action, or SDA, and served as a representative from Prijedor. Sejmenovic observed the development of the Serbian Democratic Party, or SDS, and its pursuit of ethnic separation. In Prijedor he saw the SDS demand the large majority of the land for Serbs. On 29 and 30 April 1992, Prijedor town was taken over by Serb soldiers and policemen. In May 1992, Sejmenovic and other SDA leaders met with military officers and the Prijedor SDS president at the Prijedor SDS building. The officers did almost all the talking. They demanded that the Muslims surrender several thousand weapons, and when the Muslim representatives said they did not have that many weapons one officer said, "That's your problem. If you do not do that, I will raze Kozarac to the ground." Sejmenovic observed an organised campaign of expulsion in Prijedor, including the attack on Kozarac foreshadowed by this meeting and charged at Schedule A6.1 of the indictment. Throughout Prijedor he saw the same pattern: Serb forces would surround an area, open fire from all directions, and send the survives to Omarska and Trnopolje. Numerous Muslim villages were destroyed. Eventually Sejmenovic entered Trnopolje. He heard about killings and rapes. Then six people who had helped him were killed, relevant to Scheduled Incident B13.5 and he escaped. He later snuck back into the camp but soon surrendered to save the lives of other detainees. He was then sent to Omarska. Mr. Sejmenovic's evidence about these camps is relevant to the counts of torture and cruel treatment charged at Schedules C15.2 and C15.4 of the indictment. While at Omarska, Sejmenovic was interviewed by two Serb journalists. One of them brought him a script to read and told him if he did so it would save his life. He was forced to give a false statement implicating Muslim leaders in the conflict in Prijedor. And, Your Honours, that concludes the public summary of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, in paragraph 9 of your statement - now Exhibit P283 - on page 3 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S you described the SDS claiming 70 per cent of Prijedor municipality as Serb land. How did you learn of this claim?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may just say one sentence about the document that was previously on our screens that is an ID document with a photograph. The Judge asked why there was a word handwritten in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I believe that's 65 ter 18244, now P286, if it would assist the witness to have it in front of him again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the Witness -- it was only one very small thing. If you would briefly explain, then please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can do that. When I was given that document in Banja Luka, I noticed there was a grammatical error in the sentence. The word "da" was missing and when I received this document I added the word "da" in Cyrillic in order to make this sentence sound sensible. That's why it appeared there. And now I think I can answer the question that was put to me earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbs' territorial claims were explicitly declared and became abundantly clear as soon as a Serb official in a municipal paper ordered a cadastral map of Prijedor to be printed depicting, according to them, that over 70 per cent of territory of Prijedor municipality was owned by Serbs. Seeing that map, the non-Serbs were in shock, but they didn't have either a possibility or capability to refute this map officially. The entire state assets were described as belonging to the Serbs, including natural resources, sports facilities --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I apologise for interrupting. Can you tell the Chamber in what paper that map was published?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: That was "Kozarski Vjesnik," which is the Official Gazette of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And why would you think that a map published in "Kozarski Vjesnik" was published by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Because this SDS official was at the head of this paper, and the SDS had full control of it. There was only one journalist, Muharem Nezivovic, who worked for "Kozarski Vjesnik," but at that point he didn't have any influence at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'd ask that the court reporter bring -- sorry, the court officer bring 65 ter 18281 to our screens. It's a report from the Prijedor SJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, in preparation for your testimony here, did you review this report?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And does it accurately describe the events of the evening of 29 to 30 April 1992 which you discuss in Exhibit P283, your statement?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender 65 ter 18281 into evidence as the next public Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 18281 becomes Exhibit P288, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P288 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd now ask that the court officer please call 65 ter 06951 to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: 06951. And, yes, that's the correct document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, could you look at the B/C/S version of this document on the left and read below the letter I, the first paragraph, and we're going to need to slide a little bit to the left on the document. Perhaps if there are technical difficulties showing him a large enough version to read, if I read the English and he gets the translation, that would be appropriate. In this paragraph, sir, it says: "All executive posts, posts involving a likely flow of information, posts involving the protection of public property, that is, all posts of importance to the functioning of the economy may only be held by personnel of Serbian nationality." My question to you, sir, is: Was the policy discussed in this order implemented and followed in Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and even before the date when this decision was written. It is dated the 22nd of June --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: -- whereas this process had already started in Prijedor before that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'd now tender 65 ter 06951 into evidence as a public Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 06951 becomes Exhibit P289, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P289 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd ask the court officer to now call, please, 65 ter 03266 to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, did you also review this document in preparation for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And what is reflected in this document, what event?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: This document is a decision dismissing a municipal official who was a non-Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And can you offer an opinion on whether this document is authentic based on your knowledge of the municipal government in Prijedor at the time?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: It is certainly authentic because a large number of people were dismissed from work in that same way or prevented from coming to work. In other words, all non-Serbs were prevented from coming to work or were sacked, and after a short period of time nobody was allowed to work in any of these institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you recognise the stamp at the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: That's the stamp of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor and it is signed by Dr. Milan Kovacevic, who was the president of the executive committee and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: -- that is when the power was taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I now tender 65 ter 03266 as a public Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 03266 becomes Exhibit P290, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. However, Mr. Traldi, the English version shows some handwriting numbers only which does not appear to be on the original. I don't know where they come from. I don't know what the meaning of it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, we certainly didn't intend to rely on those, but I'll look into it and report back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and if need be perhaps a clean copy would be better, but then you would need leave of the Chamber to replace the English translation by a clean one. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have several more stamped documents bearing Kovacevic's name and documenting some more cases, so it would of course be my submission this is not an isolated instance. However, to focus the evidentiary record, I will not tender those unless on cross-examination the Defence contests Mr. Sejmenovic's evidence that the policy expressed in what's now P289 was carried out in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, is there any dispute about this not being a unique document, apart from what it further means, et cetera, but is there any dispute about similar documents signed by Dr. Kovacevic to exist?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There's no dispute, Your Honour. We'll be using some of these documents from the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's hereby on the record that the parties agree on the existence or more similar documents. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Sejmenovic, I want to turn to a meeting between SDA leaders and leaders of the Serb community held in Prijedor which you discuss in your statement, now P283, beginning in paragraph 4. For Your Honours' reference that begins at the bottom of page 5 of the English and page 8 of the B/C/S. And, sir, I'm going to ask you a series of focused questions about this meeting. You say here the meeting was held at the SDS headquarters. When you arrived outside headquarters, who did you first meet?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: First we ran into several policemen, and although we had been announced and the SDS has approved our arrival and ordered the check-points to let us through because we were coming from Kozarac surrounded by police and military forces, the police still intercepted us before the premises of the SDS, asked to see our IDs and check us. They were facing people whom they knew very well, officials, but they were just intimidating us. At that point Simo Miskovic came out and invited us in. He told the policemen to stop checking our IDs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And then, I take it, you went inside. Can you describe for the Chamber the room where you and Miskovic and the others went?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: It was a large room with two smaller rooms on the side, including a kitchenette, Dusan Kurnoga was sitting there and SDS officials, Slobodan Kuruzovic also an SDS official, one person I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let's skip with the room for a moment. Were you all at one long table or were there a group of chairs distributed around the room?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: There was a long conference table. The people I enumerated were already sitting on one side. And an acquaintance of mine, Dusan Kurnoga, was in a smaller room off to the side and a girl who worked there as a secretary. We started talking but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Before we get into the conversation, where at the table was Mr. Miskovic sitting?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miskovic was sitting facing the rest of us. He occasionally stood up and walked to the smaller room, sometimes of his own accord, sometimes summoned by Mr. Kurnoga. They were expecting a fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And about how far away from you was he at the time?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Very close.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you describe in your statement that then some military officers arrived and joined the meeting. Where did Major Zeljaja sit at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Major Zeljaja was sitting in the second chair behind the table. Colonel Arsic was sitting in the first chair, next to him Major Zeljaja. And next to Zeljaja the third person they brought in sat down and he was introduced as their military security officer. Then there was Miskovic, next to Miskovic a person whose name I didn't know from the police, and next to Miskovic Slobodan Kuruzovic was sitting. On the other side of the table we were sitting in this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you say in paragraph 24 of your statement, on page 6 of the English and page 8 of the B/C/S, that the Serb military and political figures at the meeting took identical positions. Did one of them, one or the other - the military or the politicians - seem to be more in charge during the meeting, seem to be taking the lead?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Miskovic as the president of the SDS spoke very little and he did not want to begin the meeting before Colonel Arsic and Major Zeljaja arrived. We wanted to begin but he said he couldn't begin the meeting without them. When the meeting began Colonel Arsic was taking the floor most of the time in the first part of the meeting and then Major Zeljaja took over and he ended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, you discuss many of the details of what was said in your statement. So I just want to ask you one more question about this meeting. Based on your observations and the conversation during the meeting, did you develop an impression of what the Serb authorities in Prijedor intended to do next relative to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Not only did we get an impression, we were told so in so many words. At the beginning of the meeting they were playing cat and mouse with us and they made some jokes in very bad taste, at our expense; and we were very anxious, fearful, and we were hoping to -- we were looking for some hope at that meeting. However, they gave us an ultimatum. They told us how many troops they had under arms and what kind of weapons. But obviously they had not agreed beforehand so they gave us different figures. One said that there were 5.000 armed men, Zeljaja said that Kozarac had 7.000 weapons, and this security officer said he had the best information and he said in fact we have 10.000 pieces of weapons --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you just for a second. When you say "they had not agreed beforehand," are you referring to agreement on how many weapons the Muslim community had?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: -- the military security officer said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Then I want to return to the question I'd asked you a moment ago: Did you develop an impression of what they intended to do next relative to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Major Zeljaja said in so many words, I quote, "Unless you surrender 7.000 weapons, I will raze Kozarac to the ground." He repeated that several times, and that was the last thing he said. And he also added, Unless you surrender 7.000 weapons and unless the Serbian flag is flying over Kozarac and the Serb police have control, I'll raze Kozarac to the ground. And he said at the end, When you return those weapons then we can go on talking. Becir Medunjanin answered, How can we return them if we don't have them? And to that he only said, That is your problem, gentlemen, this meeting is over.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When he said, "That is you problem gentlemen," did you get an impression of what was going to happen next?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: He repeated he would raze Kozarac to the ground unless we handed over the required --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: -- number of weapons. He said we shouldn't play with him, the Banja Luka Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Next, sir, I'm going to ask you three focused questions about the attempts to expand the Kozarac TO after the meeting which you describe in P283. First, as best you can tell at its highest, about how many men were in the Kozarac TO?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean the number before the expansion of the TO or after?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The most at any point.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: In peacetime it could have numbered several hundred at most, 1- to 200, that's my rough estimate, although I'm not really qualified to make it. But in the attempt to enlarge the Territorial Defence we were still not able to boost it over a couple of hundred and this process of expansion was never finished because we neither had time nor the capability.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in paragraph 28 of P283, on page 6 of the English and page 9 of the B/C/S you talk about Serb leaders making reference to the Green Berets. As far as you knew, were there any Green Berets in Prijedor in May and June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No, there were no Green Berets or any other formation. The term "Green Berets" was used by Serb officers as propaganda without any substance to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, sir, have you heard of a village named Radmilovo in the Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Radmilovo village does not exist in the Prijedor municipality and it never did. I heard that the Serb army had renamed Kozarac into Radmilovo village after their successful operation offensive and the razing of Kozarac. It was done by Zeljaja. I heard that Zeljaja's name was Radmilo and that they renamed Kozarac after him. I was not there to see it, but I was informed that there was even a [indiscernible] at the entry into Kozarac with that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, at paragraph 40 of your statement, on page 9 of the English and page 13 of the B/C/S, you describe the destruction of non-Serb villages and say Serb-populated villages experienced little or no damage. I have only one question: Is what you say about this the distinction that I just repeated, is that based on your personal observations?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to see that myself as I was being taken out of Trnopolje to be taken to the prison in Prijedor, and when I was taken from the prison in Prijedor to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, was your own property damaged in Prijedor during this period?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have any property in Prijedor. At the time I had -- I lived in an old house and it was partly damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, I'm sorry, when I said "Prijedor" I meant to refer to the municipality rather than the town. That old house you referred to, that was within the municipality of Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And do you know during this period what happened to the mosques in Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The mosques were destroyed, usually by tanks or they were blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And when did you hear about the mosques being destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: We heard about that often from people who were deported to Trnopolje camp from various parts of Prijedor, and we heard it practically first-hand because some of those people were witnesses to that destruction. And I was able to see it myself as I was being deported from the prison in Prijedor towards Omarska. There had been a lot of mosques along that road, but not anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And do you know the name of any of the specific mosques that had previously been along that road?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Along that road was the mosque in Mujkanovici, Kozarusa, Kamicani, Jakupovici, and I've listed only some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, I'd now like to turn to your time in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'd ask the court officer to please call up 65 ter 11338.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, in your statement you described entering Trnopolje. Can you describe the physical condition of the people you saw who were held there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: In the camp I first heard only hearsay information, but when I came closer, like 700 metres from the camp, I could see people inside. They looked exhausted. They moved slowly, gazing with dull eyes. Some of them were lying on the grass because they had no accommodation, not even improvised. Later I went in and had contact with some of the people and I got more specific information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And does this picture of the detainee in the front of this picture, does this accurately reflect the state of health of the people you saw in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: This is what they looked like most of the time, most of them, because of the starvation, the beatings, and the constant fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'd ask that 65 ter 11338 be admitted into evidence as the next public Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 11338 becomes Exhibit P291, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P291 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I only have one more question about your time in Trnopolje, sir. In paragraph 47 of your statement, P283, on page 10 of the English and 15 of the B/C/S, you discuss the killing of six people with the family name Foric. Do you know the first names of any of those six people named Foric?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Three times two brothers or the children of three brothers Jasmin, Zijad, Zilhad, I cannot remember the rest. Perhaps I'd need a bit more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And for Zijad and Zilhad, are those different people or a different way of saying the same name?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Two different persons. They are the children of two different brothers. They themselves were not brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, I want to turn now to your time in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'd ask the court officer to call up 65 ter 10894.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, as you'll see, the photograph is of a model. What does the model you see here represent?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: This is the Omarska work camp. At that time it was actually a concentration camp. This is a model.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in your statement you mention seeing people sitting in an asphalt area when you arrived at Omarska. Where were you taken from that asphalt area?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I was taken inside, into this building on the right, in this photograph, or rather, the smaller building. My name and surname were recorded and then I was taken out to this small white house that is in the upper part of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And what were the conditions of the detainees you met in the white house?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The white house was covered in blood, the floors, the walls, totally covered in blood. In one room near the entrance there were a few people there lying on the floor moaning. The left room was empty, though, and the soldiers took me to the room on the left; and then a beating followed administered by the soldiers. If I remember correctly, there were five of them. They did not enter as a group, they entered one by one. And then a civilian entered the room and his task was also to administer the beating. After that they took me out, and in the meantime they called a man from the other building to wipe the blood off my face because it was covered with blood, and then they took me to this smaller building upstairs to the third office, if I remember correctly, on the right-hand side. In the office there was a man wearing civilian clothes who had arrived from Prijedor on the same bus on which they brought me, and in addition to him there were two other men in uniform there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Is that where the interrogation you describe in your statement took place?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And when the interrogation ended, did the inspector who interrogated you say he was going to share information about that interrogation with anyone else, any person or institution?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: When the interrogation was over, they -- he said that officers of the military security were coming from Banja Luka on the following day and that they would continue the interrogation and then I would sign the statement. Indeed, on the next day, two officers of the military security arrived from Banja Luka. One of them was an older man, the other one was a younger man. They were in uniform, they interrogated me, they interviewed me, but it was rather short. After that the inspector said to me, Now all of this will go before the military court. I'm done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: What will happen to you will follow after the judgement of the military court, whatever that says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, did you remain in the white house for your whole time in Omarska; that is, were you housed there?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No. After the first interrogation I was taken to a room in between that was called the glass house. It's sort of round the middle of this smaller building --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: -- it's surrounded by glass and it doesn't have a roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I'd ask that the witness be provided with a red pen for marking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, I'm going to ask you to mark three spots on the photograph. Please do not mark anything until I ask you to do so. First, do you see the asphalt area where people were being forced to sit when you arrived at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: It's this part here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, I'd ask that you wait to mark until I ask you to do so. But within that area could you mark a number 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And do you see the white house that you mentioned where you were taken early in your time at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And could you mark a number 2 next to the white house?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, finally, do you see where the glass house you mentioned would be?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And could you mark a number 3 in that area?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'd ask that 65 ter 10894 as marked by the witness be admitted into evidence as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 10894 as marked by the witness in court becomes Exhibit P292, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P292 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just get some clarification. Mr. Sejmenovic, you made a rectangle on the blue-coloured area and -- as number 1. My question to you is: Is the asphalt only inside that rectangle you made or is the asphalt the entire blue area that we see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The entire area was asphalt, but there was this one area that was chained off and that was a square. And within that confined area people sat crouching, one next to the other. So that's why I marked it as a square.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So, sir, is it correct to say from your answer, based on your answer, that the entire blue area was asphalt but the rectangle represents the area described in your statement, in P283?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. At that point in time people were only within that square and the entire area was covered with concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, in paragraph 56 of P283, it's page 12 of the English and page 18 of the B/C/S, you mention that Islam Bahonjic, Becir Medunjanin, and Mr. Medunjanin's wife were killed in Omarska. I only have one question about this paragraph. Do you know the first name of Mr. Medunjanin's wife?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Becir Medunjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: His wife, sir.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Sadeta Medunjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Mr. Sejmenovic, the last thing I want to talk to you about is your release from Omarska. First, can you tell the Chamber how you were feeling when you were first brought to meet with Vojo Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is difficult to express this feeling. You are in a pot where everything is death and death alone. And then a person appears from top political echelons and it's as if nothing had happened, tries to talk to you only about politics. Of course I was in fear, I was tense, and I thought that this was another thing I had to face before my death. I kept silent for the most part and Vojo Kupresanin spoke and this was not really a conversation it was more of a monologue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, you say in paragraph 63, on page 13 of the English and 20 of the B/C/S, that you heard Kupresanin say that he was going to provide you with some things, a suit, some money, and other things. Do you know to whom he was speaking when he said that?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was speaking to Karadzic and he told me that he had Karadzic on the line. He confirmed to him on the telephone once he brought me to Banja Luka that we had arrived to Banja Luka and Karadzic told him to get a suit for me for sure and that I should put on some weight, get proper nourishment and get some proper rest. I didn't know the actual reasons for that but very soon I found out why that was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And why did you conclude it was happening?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, I did not conclude that. A soldier who was a driver walked up to me and said, This is a good thing for you, having become a member of the Serb Assembly; however, you have to be careful because the Muslims are going to kill you. It was only then that I actually found out what was going on. Karadzic and Kupresanin needed that then, namely, through me and through other survivors, possibly, they could simulate multi-ethnic government and show that in government there were some persons who were not Serbs and that the accusations levelled by the international community were wrong; and that way they were trying to get rid of the blame for all the atrocities they had committed even until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, I'm looking at the clock and I think you asked for one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. I have three questions remaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Three brief questions, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: First, sir, in paragraph 66 at the bottom of the same page you mention 65 ter 18244, now P286, and I just ask that that be called back up to the screen. And if we could zoom in on the top left-hand corner, the relevant information is the same in the English and the B/C/S. In your statement, sir, you say you received this document in January 1993. The document itself reads January 1992, and I'd just ask you to clarify which is the correct year.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: It is 1993 and this date -- well, I focused on it only many, many years later. Actually, it was the court here that indicated that to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: -- they put a question and that was the first time I saw that this said "1992," mistakenly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Based on your contacts with Kupresanin and other Serb authorities, did you develop an impression whether they were aware of the true state of affairs in camps like Omarska and Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: They knew fully and some of them had personal insight and they were well-informed for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When they spoke to you, did any of them ever express regret over those conditions or express the intention to punish the people at the camps who were directly abusing detainees?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I find puzzling to this day is the following: Not at any point in time did I see any negative feeling in anybody's face. They were not appalled. They were not surprised. Nothing. They were facing these facts as if this were a "normal" development in war and that is how they behaved when I was in Banja Luka too. So my impression was that they all did accept what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that completes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. We'll take a break, but we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes from now. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we'll resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just one brief matter, Your Honour. We haven't received an exhibit list yet from the Defence and I imagine it's on its way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the Chamber wondered what you wanted to do with 65 ter 10894. You have to remind me of what exactly it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The marked model, I believe, Your Honour. And if I neglected to tender that, then I apologise and I'd ask permission to do it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no problem because the marked version has been saved and the 65 ter number I referred to was only the clean copy of that map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Sejmenovic. You'll now be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for clarity, since I mentioned it, we have just received the exhibit list for this witness from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Lukic. You'll find Mr. Lukic to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will begin in a reverse order by asking you a few questions about what you spoke last and then we'll move to your statement. You mentioned the map that was published and that the SDS claimed that 70 per cent of the land belonged to the Serbs. Did you, yourself, study the cadastral registers?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't but I do have some limited knowledge on that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to you, what were the respective percentages of the Muslims, the Serbs, and the Croats? Can you just tell me the percentages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Short pause between answer and question, please. And could you do the same, Mr. Sejmenovic. Could you just pause for a second between question and answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have any specific percentages?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: My supposition in that regard is as following.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Supposition. You have no knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: That is in the domain of expertise of the professionals.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Your Honours, allow me to say this. Seventy per cent of the land on the Prijedor map was socially owned property of all ethnic groups. The rest was in the private hands, and then this rest can only be divided into Muslim, Serb, and Croatian property. That was the actual state. At that time, the Serbs claimed all this common property as being their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that what they say explicitly?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: All the areas of Urije, of Kozarac, the industrial complexes were also marked in colour red on the maps and all these things were socially owned property.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Concerning Kozara [Realtime transcript read in error "Kozarac"], is it correct that there were large properties covered in woods belonging to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please do not overlap and the witness is kindly asked to begin his answer from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I -- Mr. Lukic will now repeat his question. Could you only start answering it when you see the letters on your screen are not moving any further, because otherwise the interpreters will miss part of your answer. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that non-Serbs could not refute what was published --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you were invited to repeat your last question which has not been answered. You said: "Concerning Kozarac, is it correct" --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Kozara, Kozara, that's mountain Kozara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Kozara.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, concerning Mount Kozara, whether it was correct that there were large properties covered in woods belonging to -- and could you then complete that question, belonging to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Belonging to Serbs. And could you now answer that question, Mr. Sejmenovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course there were pieces of land belonging to the Serbs, but the by far biggest part of the land was socially owned. This gentleman is insisting on title deeds that date from some previous and earlier period, but this is to be debated elsewhere. I know that in 1918 and 1928 as a result of agricultural reform a lot of the land had been confiscated, including parts of Kozara and were given to the Serbs. For example, one such place is Pasino Nikonaci [phoen] but this is not the subject here. At the time when this map was published, the categories of ownership were socially owned and private property. The map depicted at the time showed the huge part of common or socially owned property as being the ownership of the Serbs, which was in contravention of reality and the actual state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, I think you remember my instructions. This is the last warning. No speaking allowed. Communication by little notes. Consultations during the breaks. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You keep saying "at the time," "at the time when the map was published." When was the map published?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date, but that was shortly before the take-over of power that the map was published.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And are you trying to say that at the time in "Kozarski Vjesnik" there were no Muslims employees?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: At the time my friend Muharem Nezirovic worked for "Kozarski Vjesnik." And according to the information that I had, neither he nor anyone else had any impact on editorial policies and he was unable to either refute or retract any published material.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for Dr. Kovacevic, you said that he was the vice-president of the executive committee?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: He was the president of the executive committee. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, take part in the work of the Assembly of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said then that the military investigators told you that your fate depended on the conviction or the judgement that was to be rendered by the military?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, that was how it was recorded. What were you told by the military investigators?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's not what I said. I'm going to repeat what I said, and I have to react to your observation in terms that you said today I am inserting the army. Now, when I first appeared before this Tribunal in Tadic case I said that after being interrogated by Mr. Radakovic, two military security officers came from Banja Luka and they stayed there for a short period of time. You can find reference to this in at least two cases. So I'm not offering any new information today. That's the first thing. Secondly, I already spoke about this, and you can find it on record, that the investigator who questioned me, Mr. Radakovic, literally said: I am done. This is now going to be deferred to a military court. End of quotation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, would you please focus your answers on what is asked and not refer to any records which are not known to this Chamber because the parties have not provided us with it. Just try to leave comment out and only answer the question. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please have in e-court the witness's statement which is P283.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which page and paragraph, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's start with paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, in this paragraph you speak about how the SDS was established. Did you ever take part in the work of any SDS organs?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't, but I was able to hear about the existing SDS organs, either from the media or from my friends and colleagues who were holding different positions within the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it a fact that you don't know the inner workings of the SDS, how the decisions were being made and implemented?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the detailed procedure, but basically the procedure was as I described it. There was the president who was the main person, there was municipal board, sometimes there was an Executive Board. Whether the SDS had an Executive Board, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's now move to paragraph 7. You speak here about new reorganisation [as interpreted] requested by the SDS and you say that this was in the contravention of the B&H constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just in order to avoid any misunderstanding, it was "regionalisation" and not "reorganisation." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which BH constitution are you referring to, the one that was in force at the time?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the one that was in force at the time with all the inherited laws that were not readopted in the meantime and were simply adopted from the previous period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which particular constitutional provision were you referring to when you said that it was in contravention -- this regionalisation was in contravention of it?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The regionalisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina could definitely not be based on an ethnic principle. At the moment I cannot tell you the exact article of the constitution because I'm not an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. Are you familiar with chapter 5 of the BH constitution?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. You can read it out if you believe it's useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In that chapter we read, among other things, the working people and citizens - that was the language used at the time - are free to unite into associations or other socio-political organisations.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it doesn't say on ethnic grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says "free," free to associate. Let me go on with my questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just wanted to check if this has a Defence 65 ter number. It wasn't on the list we got for the witness, but if it's in e-court it would be helpful for us to be able to review it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sure it does have your 65 ter number, but I haven't marked it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We'll look around then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand the witness to be talking about regionalisation of the geographic area of the country. You're talking about freedom of association [indiscernible] associate whatever way you like but not appropriate land to yourselves as owned by that specific ground other than what is provided for in the constitution, as I understand it. What I'm trying to say to you is what you are quoting to the witness as freedom of association doesn't address what you are discussing with the witness which is regionalisation of the geographic area of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I know but I cannot testify here, that was actually the base where that regionalisation would take place on. It has nothing to do with the property, ownership, but about the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, sure --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- joining of municipalities. There was base for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not what the witness is testifying about. The witness is testifying about the fact that SDS was appropriating vast areas of land, 70 per cent of it, to the Serbs. That has nothing to do with freedom of association. It has got to do with how you divide the land.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll try to clarify, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sejmenovic, in paragraph 7 are you talking about ownership of land or are you talking about the joining of municipalities together into a region? Can you see this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: A moment. Bosnia and Herzegovina was already regionalised at the time. The regionalisation was already in place. The SDS was asking for the regionalisation to be effected in a different way, along ethnic principles, although these processes should have been regulated at the republic level, not the municipal level. The republic leadership should have taken those decisions, whereas it was done on municipal level, in Serb municipalities, and it was even called Serb autonomous region. The municipalities were not the ones who had the freedom to associate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the right to associate? Do you have any legal training, by the way?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that you cannot interpret the constitution or the constitutional provisions of the then-Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, already at your first question I made this reservation and I said I'm not qualified in these matters. But I do have some experience of work in the parliament, five years' experience, more precisely, and I know what this is about. Also, knowing that it has to deal with these issues at the state level, the SDS raised this issue in the republic assembly. They substantiated their proposal at several sessions. They tried to push through this new regionalisation at state level. These attempts were opposed for the reasons I already described here, because they wanted to round off certain ethnic territories, and this regionalisation was just a pretext.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, Mr. Lukic, before we end up in a colloquium on constitutional law, paragraph 7 expresses as the view of this witness who is not a trained lawyer, certainly not a constitutional lawyer, that what he describes as a matter of fact that he thinks it's against the BH constitution. Now, since he is not an expert, let's leave it for the time being with that and let's not enter in further debates on whether or not it's the view of this witness at this moment. Perhaps there are other moments where we could further explore that. Second, the freedom of association and the freedom to reorganise constitutional structures and administrative structures may not be exactly the same, but again not a subject perhaps to be discussed at this moment with a witness who seems not to be an expert in this matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll just clear up some facts now. Is it true that at that time the party you belonged to, the SDA, was advocating the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The party to which I belonged at the time was advocating a reorganisation of Yugoslavia from which one republic, Slovenia, had already seceded. In the eyes of the party to which I belonged, Yugoslavia was a state with its -- all of its republics, but when, for different reasons, various republics started seceding, the president of our party advocated that negotiations should be held to make some sort of state again and to avoid conflict and tensions. For the party to which I belonged, Yugoslavia without Slovenia, without Croatia, was not really Yugoslavia anymore. It was the remnant of a country in which all the balance that it had rested upon was upset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- you have not really answered the question put to you by Mr. Lukic. Could you please tell us whether it's true that at the time the SDA was advocating the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Yugoslavia; that is, that they wanted Bosnia and Herzegovina to become independent, an independent state from Yugoslavia? Is that what at the time was advocated by the SDA leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since it was a process, could counsel please pin-point the period he is referring to, the month and the year?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We were talking about 1991 regarding regionalisation. So I asked you at the time, that means in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: That was a time of intense negotiations. We were in favour of staying within Yugoslavia, however, in a Yugoslavia with all of its republics. We were against staying inside a Yugoslavia that would have only three or four republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1991 were all the republics still part of Yugoslavia, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1991, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So when I ask you about 1991, you're talking about a situation when not all the republics were there. And in that situation, was your party in favour of secession, of a separate state of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Our party held the following position: If other republics proclaim independence, we want our republic to become independent too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a reference to Mr. Traldi, the constitution of BH is 65 ter 15207, and the 1974 BH constitution is 17211.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 8 you state: "The SDS justified its attempt to create ethnically separate regions based on its goal of keeping ethnic Serbs in Yugoslavia and did not take into account the views of other political parties." At that time did the SDA take into account the positions of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you gave up on secession because the SDS wanted it to remain one state; right?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: The SDA had a basis for its activity and any activity it pursued, it pursued through parliamentary procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's enough. I've let you talk around quite enough. Even the Prosecutor kept you focused on his questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, that's not the language -- I've let you talk around quite enough -- you can interrupt, but no problem. But most important, take a short pause between answer and question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have no time to take a pause, Your Honour, because the witness is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you take --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- talking all the time. I have to stop him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you do that with one or two words, Stop here, please, or I have to interrupt you. And then leave it to that until the witness stops. If he doesn't do that, I will assist you in achieving that aim.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sejmenovic, if your answer is not sufficiently focused on the question, Mr. Lukic may interrupt you and then you'll have to stop and then you should listen to his next question as you have to do now. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you say the SDS justified its attempt to create ethnically separate regions by its goal of keeping ethnic Serbs in Yugoslavia and did not want to take into account the views of other political parties. My question is: Did the SDA take into account the efforts of the SDS to remain within Yugoslavia or not?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN SEJMENOVIC
utterances.text: Everything was taking place in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The SDS did not have a majority in the parliament and its proposals were against the will of the parliamentary majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm looking at the clock --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and unfortunately we have to stop for the day. Mr. Sejmenovic, I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in any other way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or whether that's testimony you will give tomorrow. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 and you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that there is a practical problem with 65 ter 22696 which was admitted, but it being a video I think there's a problem that the CD is not provided to the Registrar. So we have to pay further attention to that. But let's do that -- yes, perhaps under those circumstances we should change the status in P287 to be marked for identification until the matter has been resolved, preferably out of court. If there's no other matter, we adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 3rd of October, at 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 3rd day of October, 2012, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.15 p.m.,
